subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY-TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY-TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether his understanding^ is the same as my own with respect to the taking up of estimates on Thursday and Friday. I understood last night that the Prime Minister wished to proceed to-day with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce and expressed the view that that might have to be by consent. Let me say at once that so far as the official opposition is concerned we are quite agreeable to proceeding to-day with the estimates of that department by consent. My inquiry at the moment is as to whether it will be necessary or not for the estimates of all other departments to be taken up in committee of supply on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday before they can be taken up, except by consent, on Thursday or Friday. I believe that last night, from his remarks, the Prime Minister may have had in mind that the house having taken up in supply some supplementary estimates of the fiscal year 1932-33, we might be considered as having already entered upon the estimates of these particular departments. My reading of the
Business of the House

rule is that unless a department has had its estimates gone into before a Thursday or Friday, it cannot, except by consent, have its estimates considered on a Thursday or Friday, and that this applies to the main estimates of the session and not to supplementary estimates pertaining to a previous fiscal year. If there is any doubt about this, perhaps His Honour the Speaker would give a ruling on the matter.
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime
Minister): It was because I was somewhat uncertain about the matter myself that I mentioned it last night as I did. Had it not been for that uncertainty it would have been unnecessary to have brought it to the attention of the house. The fact is that this house as at present constituted has already resolved itself into committee of supply and that committee of supply has considered the estimates of several of the departments, including Trade and Commerce. It is equally true that the estimates considered were supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1933, and I was somewhat uncertain as to whether, reading the rule, you could not technically say that the obligation had been discharged when the house was in committee on the estimates of any department on Thursday and Friday, as in fact was the case. It is true that in the early days of this session we passed a motion suspending the operation of the rules, whereby it became possible to have every day regarded as a government day. That is clear. I think it would probably be the sense of the house that it would be a more equitable observance of the rule if we treated the supply that was granted, by referring the items of several departments to the committee, on supplementary estimates, as not having reference to the main estimates. That would strike me as the more equitable view; if I were in the opposition I would take that view. That is the reason I mentioned it last night as 1 did, and by consent we will take up Trade and Commerce and observe the rule hereafter as though the supplementary estimates had not comprised the estimates of any department that had to be referred to the committee for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1934.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY-TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES
speechtext:
That is entirely satisfactory. My impression is that, at the time the house passed the resolution to which my right hon. friend has referred, a reservation of the kind mentioned was made by the opposition. There is one other point which I should like to have understood between us before we discuss the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is the same point that arose last year with respect

to the ten per cent deduction from the salaries of the civil service. As hon. members will have noticed by the estimates, apparently the intention is to continue the ten per cent deduction this year, though I understood last year from the government that the deduction was to be for one year only, and that it would not apply to the present year. I am not raising that point at the moment however. My question now is whether the government should not in the first instance introduce its bill, authorizing the ten per cent deduction and let us settle the matter of principle, which will be necessary on the bill, rather than attempt to settle it item by item as we discuss the estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY-TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES
speechtext:
It is not proposed to
vote in the aggregate a sum greater than ninety per cent of what the figure heretofore has been. It will be observed that at the end of each item a deduction of ten per cent is made, so that the vote will be only for ninety per cent of the salaries as they were prior to last year. That is my understanding of the situation after the discussion I have had with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). I cannot see that it will make any difference inasmuch as the amount available under the action of the committee for the purposes of discharging the public services will be only the sums mentioned in the final estimates, as indicated by the document tabled yesterday. If it would affect in any sense the principle, I could understand there being some importance in passing the legislation, but as it stands I cannot see that it would be necessary to do so.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES ON THURSDAY AND FRIDAY-TEN PER CENT DEDUCTION FROM CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES
speechtext:
It does affect
the principle. This house this year has not decided that the salaries of the civil servants shall be cut ten per cent, and until the house does so decide I do not think we should by any act, either implied or otherwise, countenance that action. The same point was raised last year and the government admitted eventually that the course of procedure which I urged should be followed was the correct one. While we were discussing the items under trade and commerce we withheld any which affected salaries until after the government had brought in its bill and the bill had passed this house. All I am asking is that the same procedure shall be followed this year.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEYENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: QUESTION OP PRINTING TRADE AND COMMERCE BULLETINS IN ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these bulletins are really brief editorial presentations of what otherwise would be technical reports
which emerge from time to time from the bureau of statistics. They are put out for press circulation to facilitate the distribution of information to the public through the press. Up to the present time there has been no necessity for their being printed in the French language, and to do so would double the cost of production without perhaps adding anything effective to their value. My hon. friends will please bear in mind that these are specially distributed to the members of the press gallery.

subtopic: QUESTION OP PRINTING TRADE AND COMMERCE BULLETINS IN ENGLISH AND FRENCH

Some of the members
of the press gallery are French speaking and they have not time to make a translation.

Up to the present this subject has not been brought to my attention other than by a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). If it is thought desirable that these bulletins should be printed in French as well as English, we will endeavour to do so, although I would point out that it will double the cost.

Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Publication.
The minister might explain the significance of this section.

The proposed amendment is the result of a request of the law clerks 
of the house. I think I could not do better than read the letter which was submitted by Messrs. Troop and Ollivier on June 26, 1928, to the Deputy Minister of Justice. This letter reads:
Dear Mr. Edwards:
The statutes of 1928 are being printed rapidly and we are comparing and correcting the proofs.
There is a serious matter to which you will allow us to draw your attention in this respect.
By section 46 (2) of the Fisheries Act, Revised Statutes, chapter 73, by section 4 (3) of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, Revised Statutes, chapter 100, the regulations under these acts are to be printed in the prefix to the annual volume of the statutes. We have had to do this for years past and it is the cause of delay in getting out of the statutes. This year is worse than usual, as we have to print again the special fishery regulations for each province, a small volume in themselves, besides the amending regulations. The migratory birds regulations are not so long.
Some years ago, when Sir Lomer Gouin was Minister of Justice, we brought this to his attention and he advised us to leave the regulations out if any delay was caused in issuing the statutes. We asked him to bring in a bill to amend these two acts, to delete these provisions, but it was overlooked.
These regulations are printed in the Canada Gazette and printed and distributed widely by the departments concerned. They are printed for the third time in our annual volume.
We will be sending this prefix to the printing bureau to-morrow, and would like just to show it to you before doing so, and you will understand the point clearly. Mr. Troop will call in and it will only take a moment of your time.
Yours sincerely,
Troop and Ollivier, Law Clerks.
W. Stuart Edwards, K.C.,
Deputy Minister of Justice,
Ottawa.
That is the reason for this proposed amendment; it is merely to meet the wishes of the law clerks so as to enable the statutes to be printed at an earlier date than is otherwise possible.

Just for the purpose of information, may I ask the minister; if these regulations are not printed annually in the statutes, in what manner will the public be informed, because practically nobody outside of the lawyers reads the Canada Gazette?
And not many of them do so.

Some of them had splendid war records, and it does seem strange to me that they should be let out and new men taken on to replace them, especially in view of the order in council transferring them to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That has been done before, as I say, but in very exceptional oases. I have never approved of it. I do not believe it is the proper thing; it is an ingenious way of getting rid of the act. I criticize the item first on the ground that it is not in accordance with the principle of economy which should be practised at this time; second that there is an increase in the salary of $3,000, and third, that it is a contravention of the Civil Service Act.

I fear I cannot allow the observations my hon. friend has made to go without an answer. In the first place there is not an increase. The situation is this; Mr. Wilgress was at Hamburg. There is an increase in

Mr. STEVENS; When I said I had no apology to make it was not with any desire to affront the house, but rather to assure the house of my conviction of the rightness of the course I had taken and that I am quite willing to take full responsibility for it. Mr. LaVERGNE: Has the minister considered the desirability of raising the trade commissioners to the position of consul in countries where they represent Canada? I understand that our trade commissioners are in an inferior position in other countries where they have the position virtually of consuls.

I have given a great deal of thought to that suggestion. Quite a number of prominent and competent persons in Canada have made the suggestion and after giving it a good deal of consideration I came to the conclusion that it would not be wise. In saying that I am expressing my own opinion. Of course, such a change would necessitate action on the part of the government and I am now speaking not the opinion of the Prime Minister but merely my own as head of this department. The reason I came to that conclusion was this. The primary object of a trade commissioner abroad is trade, business, making contacts between Canadian business houses and prospective customers, the compilation of information on trade and all matters appertaining to trade; and the danger is that if you make the trade commissioner a diplomatic officer he will become obsessed with a glorified idea of his position, and I do not say this at all offensively.
A superiority complex.

Yes; he might develop a diplomatic complex and might pay more attention to the diplomatic than to the trade side of his duties. The only objection is that the trade commissioner in a foreign country, in approaching the government, has more difficulty achieving that objective, that is to say, getting direct contact with the minister than has the consul of another country. That is true; but we must bear in mind that the 
major part of the trade commissioner's duties consists not in contacts with the government, negotiating between one government and the other, but in contacts between business men in Canada and business men in the country in which he is stationed. While, therefore, I am not adamant on this, I came to the conclusion that it would be better for our trade commissioners to retain the status of purely commercial rather than diplomatic agents.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I always understood
that a consul's occupation had relation more to trade. Diplomacy is represented by ministers or ambassadors, but the consul's function relates more to trade. Coming down to the business side of it, on looking over the list of Canadian trade agents I find very few French names. I state openly at this time that I do not think a man should be appointed to any position because of his nationality; qualification should come first, but he should not be kept out of any position because of his French descent. In many countries in South America, in Europe and in Africa the qualification for a foreign trade agent is that he shall be able to speak the language of the particular country, or French. I could name forty-two countries where that qualification is necessary. I am wondering just how many of our thirty-five agents are familiar with the French language and are therefore able adequately to represent this country in trade matters. In many countries French is the language which replaces the language of the country when that is not known to the individual. I am sure that outside of the agents at Brussels, Paris and Cairo, very few of our trade representatives abroad are familiar with the French language. I understand that in Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Peru where a trade agent does not speak Spanish, he conducts his negotiations in the French language. Knowledge of French is a qualification which should be necessary in the appointment of our trade agents.

I might say to my hon. friend that I feel just as responsible for these trade commissioners as does the minister. I think my hon. friend is making a mistake when he assumes that our trade commissioners do not know the languages of the countries in which they are located. That is one of the first requirements of a man to be sent to a foreign field. I am not saying that Mr. Langley can speak Japanese, or that Mr. Cosgrave can speak Chinese, as they might be the exceptions. I should like to support what the minister has said against giving diplomatic status to our trade commissioners.

Great Britain and Europe, up to the time Great Britain put a tax of one shilling four pence per gallon upon cod oil, were the natural markets for Norwegian and Swedish oil, but since that tax was put on very little of this oil has gone into Great Britain and the other countries of Europe. Canadian cod oil found a natural market in the United States, but due to this policy of interfering with trade, the Norwegians immediately looked for other markets. They came to the United States, and to-day we find Norwegian cod oil coming to Boston and New York while Canadian cod oil crosses the Atlantic to Great Britain.

I should like to make one or two suggestions to the Minister in connection with our trade services abroad. I think we

are neglecting a great market in not having trade agents in Russia. We cannot afford to miss any of these opportunities. When the minister looks over the cost of our foreign business, he has to go beyond the cost of administering the commercial intelligence service and to turn t-o the amount of money Canada votes for subventions to steamships plying between. The minister was good enough this afternoon to give some figures of the export of lumber from Canada to Australia. I noticed in answer to a question asked by myself and which the minister answered that

a subsidized service to China at the present time which is finding a market for a class of lumber which is very difficult to market in Canada or Great Britain-in fact cannot be marketed there-that known as common. That service is very successful, carrying a great deal of lumber to that market.
There is at present no subsidy for the service to Australia. There was a subsidy under a contract entered into about four or five years ago to Australia, but that contract expired last year. For the last three years the subsidy was paid for a service to China, not to Australia; but during the past year the increase of lumber shipments to which my hon. friend refers was largely, or entirely due, to the additional preference secured under the trade agreement with Australia.

With all d'ue regpect I think I am quite in order in referring to the fact that some $268,950 was paid from August, 1929, to December, 1932, to ships carrying lumber from Canada. My reason for saying I am in order is that the minister this afternoon was good enough to give full particulars regarding exports of lumber from this country. In my question which appears on page 1686 of Hansard I asked:
1. What amount has been paid by the Dominion of Canada to ships carrying lumber from British Columbia ports?
And the answer given was, $268,950. I have no objection to the shipments of lumber being increased, but I say that every port of this country' should be treated alike. If it is thought advisable that steamships should be subsidized to carry' lumber from British Columbia ports to Australia, then it seems to me that Atlantic ports and Atlantic shippers of lumber should be put in the same position. It is not quite fair if no money has been paid by this government for subsidies to encourage the lumber trade from Atlantic coast ports. The government should seriously consider this matter and put all our ports on the same basis.

We all recognize these days the difficulties in the w.ay of international trade, on account of the high tariffs different countries have put into effect and the barriers of extreme nationalism. We recognize that it is necessary' for this country and all countries that are endeavouring to trade with one another to have agents, ambassadors, consuls in the different countries to promote trade. I hold in my hand a clipping from a newspaper which purports to lay before the people the new deal which the president-elect of the

United States proposes to put into effect. His program is arranged under seven heads, and I notice that the seventh is: "Restoring foreign trade by' general debt-tariff adjustments, and by Business with Russia." Arising out of that I would like to ask the minister what steps his government is taking to promote trade with Russia. Llave we any agents there? Are we doing anything at all to promote trade? Russia seems to be the one country in the world that many nations are looking to for trade. Are we doing anything at all along those lines?

The document presented to the house by the Prime Minister the other day I think covers the situation. There is little I can add to what was said by him in that official statement. However, my hon. friend and others who have made reference to Russian trade should bear in mind certain facts. The first is that all exports and imports of Russia are under the direct control of the government of Russia. The second is that during the past five years Russian purchases have almost invariably been based on long term credits, or what in ordinary trade would be considered long term, that is, from say eighteen months to as much as three years. The question of the extending of credits to Russia by the countries from which these goods are exported, either by a private exporter or a private exporter assisted or guaranteed by the government, is a matter of grave importance. Up to the present time this government has not considered it advisable or desirable that we should place this country's resources or credit behind the financing of the sale of goods to Russia. I grant that the subject is one for discussion; much may be said upon it. But I do not think that at the moment, and under existing circumstances, much can be said strongly in support of it. It is not my desire to reflect in any sense upon Russian methods; those are of their own choice. It is equally clear, however, that the question whether or not the government of Canada shall place its resources behind goods that leave this country to go to Russia is one that we ourselves must decide, and up to the present we have not decided in favour of it.

I thank the minister for his pronouncement. When he says that the government of Russia does all the trading in that country, we recognize that fact, and that makes it all the easier. We have not to travel all over the country to see various individuals; we go to the government. We have only to interview them; we do not need a band of agents throughout the country. But I understand that in many cases Russia is willing to

barter, in the purchase of steel rails and cattle, for example, to barter oil. Is the government willing that we shall trade on a fair basis with those people? Will it give anyone who wants to trade with them a clear bill so that they may be allowed to do it?
